summary.text: Introduce the integer recurrence \(c_{n+2}=-4c_{n+1}-64c_n\) and its half \(d_n\), and prove from the recurrences that \(4a_n=8\cdot8^n-8(-8)^n+c_n\). Writing \(c_n=r^{n+1}+s^{n+1}\) for the roots of \(x^2+4x+64\), with \(rs=64\), gives \(c_n^2=c_{2n+1}+128\cdot64^n\); the two geometric terms at an odd index contribute the same \(128\cdot64^n\), so \(4a_{2n+1}=c_n^2=(2d_n)^2\) and hence \(a_{2n+1}=d_n^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
a_{k+4}=-4a_{k+3}+256a_{k+1}+4096a_k.
\]
We prove that for every nonnegative integer \(n\), the odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((c_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
c_0=-4,\qquad c_1=-112,
\]
and
\[
c_{k+2}=-4c_{k+1}-64c_k\qquad(k\ge 0).
\]
We will need three facts about this sequence.

First, \(c_n\) also satisfies the fourth-order recurrence occurring in the definition of \(a_n\). Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{k+4}
  &=-4c_{k+3}-64c_{k+2}\\
  &=-4c_{k+3}-64(-4c_{k+1}-64c_k)\\
  &=-4c_{k+3}+256c_{k+1}+4096c_k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
c_{k+4}=-4c_{k+3}+256c_{k+1}+4096c_k. \tag{1}
\]

Second, we establish the formula
\[
4a_n=8\cdot 8^n-8\cdot(-8)^n+c_n \qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{2}
\]
To check the four initial cases, first calculate from the recurrence for \(c_n\) that
\[
c_2=-4(-112)-64(-4)=704
\]
and
\[
c_3=-4(704)-64(-112)=4352.
\]
For \(n=0\), the right-hand side of (2) is
\[
8-8-4=-4=4a_0.
\]
For \(n=1\), it is
\[
8\cdot 8-8\cdot(-8)-112=64+64-112=16=4a_1.
\]
For \(n=2\), it is
\[
8\cdot 8^2-8\cdot(-8)^2+704=512-512+704=704=4a_2.
\]
For \(n=3\), it is
\[
8\cdot 8^3-8\cdot(-8)^3+4352
=4096+4096+4352=12544=4a_3.
\]

Now each of the sequences \(8^n\), \((-8)^n\), and \(c_n\) satisfies the same fourth-order recurrence
\[
x_{k+4}=-4x_{k+3}+256x_{k+1}+4096x_k.
\]
For \(c_n\), this is (1). For a geometric sequence \(x_n=t^n\), this assertion is the identity
\[
t^4=-4t^3+256t+4096,
\]
which holds for both \(t=8\) and \(t=-8\). Explicitly, for \(t=8\), the right-hand side is
\(-4\cdot512+256\cdot8+4096=4096=8^4\), and for \(t=-8\), it is
\(-4(-512)+256(-8)+4096=4096=(-8)^4\).
Consequently the right-hand side of (2), as a function of \(n\), satisfies the recurrence defining \(4a_n\). Since equality holds at four consecutive initial indices, induction through the recurrence proves (2) for every \(n\ge 0\).

Third, we prove the doubling identity
\[
c_n^2=c_{2n+1}+128\cdot64^n. \tag{3}
\]
For this, consider the two complex numbers
\[
r=-2+i\sqrt{60},\qquad s=-2-i\sqrt{60}.
\]
Equivalently, \(s=-4-r\). Since \(i^2=-1\) and \((\sqrt{60})^2=60\), we have
\[
r+s=-4
\]
and
\[
rs=(-2)^2+(\sqrt{60})^2=4+60=64.
\]
Thus \(r\) and \(s\) are the two roots of
\[
x^2+4x+64=0.
\]
In particular,
\[
r^2=-4r-64,\qquad s^2=-4s-64. \tag{4}
\]
Multiplying (4) by the appropriate powers shows that, for every \(m\ge0\),
\[
r^{m+2}=-4r^{m+1}-64r^m,
\qquad
s^{m+2}=-4s^{m+1}-64s^m. \tag{5}
\]

We claim that
\[
c_n=r^{n+1}+s^{n+1} \qquad(n\ge0). \tag{6}
\]
For \(n=0\), the right-hand side is \(r+s=-4=c_0\). For \(n=1\), it is
\[
r^2+s^2=(r+s)^2-2rs=(-4)^2-2\cdot64=16-128=-112=c_1.
\]
By (5), the sequence \(r^{n+1}+s^{n+1}\) satisfies
\[
(r^{n+3}+s^{n+3})=-4(r^{n+2}+s^{n+2})-64(r^{n+1}+s^{n+1}),
\]
which is exactly the recurrence defining \(c_n\). Therefore induction from the two initial values proves (6).

We may now square (6):
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_n^2
 &=\bigl(r^{n+1}+s^{n+1}\bigr)^2\\
 &=r^{2n+2}+s^{2n+2}+2r^{n+1}s^{n+1}\\
 &=r^{2n+2}+s^{2n+2}+2(rs)^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (6) with index \(2n+1\),
\[
r^{2n+2}+s^{2n+2}=c_{2n+1},
\]
and since \(rs=64\),
\[
2(rs)^{n+1}=2\cdot64^{n+1}=128\cdot64^n.
\]
This proves (3).

It remains to identify an integer square root. Define another integer sequence \((d_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
d_0=-2,\qquad d_1=-56,
\]
and
\[
d_{k+2}=-4d_{k+1}-64d_k\qquad(k\ge0).
\]
We claim
\[
c_n=2d_n \qquad(n\ge0). \tag{7}
\]
This holds initially because \(c_0=-4=2(-2)=2d_0\) and \(c_1=-112=2(-56)=2d_1\). If it holds at two consecutive indices \(k\) and \(k+1\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{k+2}
 &=-4c_{k+1}-64c_k\\
 &=-4(2d_{k+1})-64(2d_k)\\
 &=2(-4d_{k+1}-64d_k)\\
 &=2d_{k+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (7) follows by induction. In particular, all the \(c_n\) are even, and \(d_n\) is an integer.

We now specialize the closed formula (2) to an odd index \(2n+1\). The elementary power identities
\[
8^{2n+1}=8(8^2)^n=8\cdot64^n
\]
and
\[
(-8)^{2n+1}=(-8)((-8)^2)^n=-8\cdot64^n
\]
give
\[
\begin{aligned}
4a_{2n+1}
 &=8\cdot8^{2n+1}-8\cdot(-8)^{2n+1}+c_{2n+1}\\
 &=8(8\cdot64^n)-8(-8\cdot64^n)+c_{2n+1}\\
 &=128\cdot64^n+c_{2n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By the doubling identity (3), the last expression is \(c_n^2\). Therefore
\[
4a_{2n+1}=c_n^2.
\]
Using \(c_n=2d_n\) from (7), we obtain
\[
4a_{2n+1}=(2d_n)^2=4d_n^2.
\]
Cancelling the nonzero integer factor \(4\) yields
\[
a_{2n+1}=d_n^2.
\]
Since \(d_n\in\mathbb Z\), this exhibits \(a_{2n+1}\) as a perfect square for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as required.
